questions.question: What is Euclidean distance measuring between two points?
options: The straight-line length of the displacement vector.
The number of coordinates in the larger point
The signed change in only the first coordinate.
The sum of the two position vectors

questions.question: Why do squared coordinate differences appear in the Euclidean distance formula?
options: They turn points into matrices
They give a length independent of sign.
They make negative distances possible
They remove all but the first coordinate.

questions.question: When is the Euclidean distance between two points equal to $0$?
options: Whenever the coordinate sums agree
Exactly when the two points are the same
Exactly when both points have positive coordinates
Whenever the points lie on a line

questions.question: How is distance from a point to a line defined in this setting?
options: The minimum Euclidean distance from the point to the line.
As the distance to any endpoint of the line
As the length of the direction vector of the line.
As the largest coordinate of the point

questions.question: Why is $d(x,y)$ the same as $d(y,x)$?
options: Because distance ignores all coordinates after the first
Because the square root changes sign when order changes
Because $x-y$ and $y-x$ have the same norm
Because $x-y=y-x$ for all points

questions.question: Compute $d((1,1),(2,2))$.
options: $\sqrt2$

questions.question: What is the distance from $(3,4)$ to the origin in $\mathbb R^2$?
Which points on the $x$-axis are distance $2$ from $(3,0)$?
What is the displacement vector used in $d(x,y)$?
options: $x-y$ or equivalently $y-x$ up to sign
The vector of coordinate sums
The zero vector for all pairs of points
The coordinatewise product of $x$ and $y$

questions.question: How does Euclidean distance differ from adding absolute coordinate changes?
options: It ignores diagonal movement
It uses only positive coordinates
The root of the sum of squared coordinate changes.
It is always larger than the taxicab sum.

questions.question: Why is the square root needed in the formula for $d(x,y)$?
options: Without it negative distances would appear
It removes the need for coordinate differences.
It changes vectors into points
Without it the formula gives squared length, not length.

questions.question: Which point on the $x$-axis is closest to $(2,3)$?
What is the minimum distance from $(2,3)$ to the $x$-axis?
Why is the distance from a point to a line not usually found by choosing an arbitrary point on the line?
options: Because the direction vector always has length zero.
Because a line has no points in Euclidean space
Because every point on a line is equally close
Because the definition uses the minimum over all points on the line

questions.question: What does the equation $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ emphasise?
options: Distance between points is computed as the length of a vector
The norm symbol means coordinatewise multiplication
The two points must be equal
Distance is a vector rather than a number

questions.question: Let $L=\{(t,0):t\in\mathbb R\}$. What is the distance from $(3,4)$ to $L$?
For the line $L=\{(t,t):t\in\mathbb R\}$, what is the distance from $(1,0)$ to $L$?
options: $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$
$\sqrt2$
